questions.question: Using a two-country table, distinguish absolute from comparative advantage and demonstrate that trade benefits both countries even when one is better at producing everything.
questions.expected_answer: Absolute advantage means producing a good with fewer resources — more output per worker. Comparative advantage means having the lowest opportunity cost — sacrificing least in other goods forgone — and it, not absolute advantage, drives the gains from trade. Example: with identical resources South Africa can produce 80 tons of citrus or 20 tons of electronics; South Korea 100 tons of citrus or 200 tons of electronics. Korea is absolutely better at both. But a ton of electronics costs South Africa four tons of citrus while it costs Korea only half a ton; a ton of citrus costs Korea two tons of electronics but costs South Africa only a quarter of a ton. Korea's smallest sacrifice is in electronics, South Africa's in citrus. If each specialises where its sacrifice is least and they trade at a ratio between the two opportunity costs — say one for one — both countries consume beyond their own production frontiers. Trade requires only differences in relative costs, not superiority.

questions.question: Set out the accounts of the balance of payments with typical South African items, and explain how the rand's exchange rate is determined on the foreign exchange market, including the correct use of depreciation, appreciation, devaluation and revaluation.
questions.expected_answer: The current account records present trade and income: merchandise exports (minerals, vehicles, fruit) and imports (oil, machinery, electronics), whose difference is the trade balance; services such as freight and tourism (a foreign visitor's spending here is a service export); income flows such as dividends and interest; and current transfers like remittances. The small capital transfer account holds items like debt forgiveness. The financial account shows how net imports are financed: direct investment (a foreign carmaker building a plant — lasting ownership), portfolio investment (foreign purchases of shares and bonds — hot money, reversible in an afternoon) and other investment (loans and deposits). The Reserve Bank's gold and foreign-exchange reserves are the shock absorber so the statement balances; a current-account deficit requires a financial-account surplus. The exchange rate is the rand price of foreign currency, set where demand for dollars (importers, travellers abroad, firms servicing dollar debt, residents investing overseas) meets supply of dollars (export earnings, arriving tourists, foreign investment inflows). Demand shifting right — heavy wheat imports in a drought — raises the rand price of the dollar: depreciation. Supply shifting right — a bumper citrus season or bond inflows — lowers it: appreciation. Devaluation and revaluation are reserved for deliberate resets under a fixed system; the rand floats freely.

questions.question: Define a balance-of-payments disequilibrium and evaluate the four channels for correcting a persistent deficit, ending with how a surplus is treated.
questions.expected_answer: A disequilibrium exists when deficits or surpluses persist beyond what routine financing can carry: chronic deficits drain reserves and pile up foreign debt; chronic surpluses mean the country consumes less than it produces while partners accumulate matching deficits. Channel one, the exchange rate: under floating, excess demand for foreign currency slides the rand down, making exports cheaper abroad and imports dearer at home so volumes adjust; cost — imported inflation and a lag before export volumes respond. Channel two, demand management: contractionary monetary and fiscal policy cools spending and hence imports, while higher rates attract financing inflows; cost — slower growth and unemployment, curing the deficit by making the patient poorer. Channel three, direct controls: tariffs, quotas and exchange control ration imports and foreign currency; cost — retaliation, evasion, inefficiency, and WTO limits. Channel four, borrowing and reserves: run down reserves or take IMF loans to buy time; cost — debt and conditionality. A surplus runs the toolkit in reverse: allow appreciation, expand domestic demand, liberalise imports. Top answers match the tool to the cause: overvalued currency — channel one; overheated economy — channel two.
